narrative:
The model predicts you have a 44% chance of failing your final year, which is high enough that the school requires you to take remedial courses to strengthen your chances of success.

The three factors that most influenced this decision were your lack of desire to pursue higher education, your study habits, and your clean record of no past failures. Wanting to continue studying after school was by far the strongest signal. Almost every student who passed expressed a clear ambition for higher education, yet you indicated you do not. This absence of long-term motivation pulled the prediction strongly toward failure.

Your limited weekly study time of less than two hours also pushed the outcome toward failing. Most students who passed dedicate two to five hours or more, so your shorter sessions made success less likely in the model’s eyes.

Interestingly, having zero past class failures worked in your favor and pulled the prediction back toward passing. This shows the system recognizes your previous academic consistency.

To improve, the clearest step is to seriously reflect on your goals. If you can reconnect with a reason to aim higher, that shift alone could dramatically change your trajectory. Pair this with increasing your regular study time—even modest extra hours each week would align you closer to the patterns of students who succeed. These two changes give you the best chance of moving from the remedial track to passing on your own.
